data_section_full_text:
Research design
Following prior audit fee research, ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions are
estimated for testing the hypotheses. A number of control variables in audit fee
models are included to control for client size, audit complexity, and client risk
(Simunic 1980; Gul and Tsui 1998). Client size is normally measured by the natural logarithm of total assets, while the current ratio, inventory, year-end month,
number of subsidiaries, and extent of overseas activities are proxies for audit complexity. The variables used to control for client risk include debt, quick ratio, audit
opinion, loss, and return on assets. Audit quality is also proxied by a dummy variable coded 1 for Big 6 audit firms and 0 for all other audit firms. Prior studies show
that these control variables have good explanatory power and are robust across different time periods, samples, and countries. The cross-sectional modified Jones
1991 model (see Bartov, Gul, and Tsui 2000) is used to measure the absolute value
of DAs. We also include in the regressions a dummy variable, INC, for incomeincreasing ( = 1) and income-decreasing accruals ( = 0), since income-increasing
accruals may be perceived by auditors to be riskier than income-decreasing ones.
Managerial ownership is proxied by a dichotomous variable with a cutoff point of
5 percent of inside directors’ share ownership to identify firms with low managerial ownership, which is consistent with prior studies (Rosenstein and Wyatt 1997;
Morck et al. 1988; Bhagat and Black 1999). In sensitivity tests, we also use different cutoff levels and measure managerial ownership as a continuous variable.
Finally, we use inside directors’ remuneration to proxy for accounting-based management compensation in the audit fee model. For this purpose, the sample is
divided into high and low compensation groups. A dichotomous variable is coded
1 (high) for firms whose ratios of compensation to total assets rank among the top
quartile in the sample and the rest are coded 0 (low). The rationale for the high cutoff of 75 percent is to capture firms that are likely to be associated with a high proportion of accounting-based management compensation. Managers of these firms
are expected to have more incentives to manage earnings opportunistically since
their compensation is dependent on accounting earnings. An implicit assumption is
that management compensation is largely explained by the firm’s size (total assets)
and that management compensation is likely to be performance-based if this ratio
is very high. This assumption is supported by the significant positive correlation
(0.23) between management compensation over total assets and return on assets
(after deleting firms with negative earnings). In the sensitivity tests, management
compensation is also measured as a continuous variable.

Model specification
The model used to test the hypotheses is as follows:

+ b 14 INC*DISC + b 15 C + b 16 C*DISC + b 17 M + b 18 C*M
+ b 19 DISC + b 20 M*DISC + b 21 C*M*DISC (1),


where


Dependent variable

FEES = the natural logarithm of total audit fees;


Control variables

SIZE = the natural logarithm of the client’s total assets;

YE = a dummy variable, 1 if the fiscal year-end is December 31, and 0

otherwise;

FOR = the percentage of subsidiaries incorporated outside Australia;

DE = the book value of long-term debt divided by total assets;

SUB = the natural logarithm of the number of subsidiaries; <sup>7</sup>

ROA = income before extraordinary items divided by the previous year’s

total assets;

AUDIT = a dummy variable, 1 if the firm is a Big 6 audit firm, and 0

otherwise;

CR = the ratio of current assets to current liabilities;

AR = the ratio of accounts receivable to total assets;

INV = the ratio of inventory to total assets;

LOSS = a dummy variable, 1 if a net loss occurred at least once in past three

years, and 0 otherwise;

OPINION = a dummy variable, 1 if the opinion is qualified, and 0 otherwise;

INC = a dummy variable, 1 if DAs are income-increasing, and 0 otherwise;

INC*DISC = the interaction between INC and DISC ;

C = a dummy variable, 1 if the ratio of inside directors’ remuneration to

total assets ranks among the top quartile of the sample, and 0
otherwise;

C*DISC = the interaction between C and DISC ;

M = a dummy variable, 1 if the percentage of shares held by inside

directors is greater than 5 percent, and 0 otherwise;

C*M = the interaction between C and M ;


CAR Vol. 20 No. 3 (Fall 2003)

Discretionary Accounting Accruals, Managers’ Incentives, and Audit Fees 449


Experimental variables

DISC = the absolute value of DAs;

M*DISC = the interaction between M and DISC ; and

C*M*DISC = the three-way interaction among C, M, and DISC .


DISC tests Hypothesis 1. The interaction ( C*DISC ) between management
compensation ( C ) and DAs is included to capture the effect of accounting-based
management compensation on the relationship between audit fees and DAs. M and
its interaction with DISC ( M*DISC ) are included in the model to test Hypothesis 2.
C*M*DISC is the three-way interaction among C, M, and DISC for testing Hypothesis 3. The interaction ( C*M ) between management compensation and management
ownership is included as a control variable to facilitate the testing of the three-way
interaction term ( C*M*DISC ). As discussed earlier, M and C are initially measured as dichotomous variables and subsequently as continuous variables in sensitivity tests. The other control variables are included in prior audit fee studies
(Simunic 1980; Gul and Tsui 1998).

Data sources
We collect financial information from the Australian Stock Exchange data file for
1993 and from annual reports. Table 1 reports the sample selection results. The
data file contains 865 firms. After deleting companies with missing values, 648
firms remain in the file, which represents 75 percent of the population. Australian
annual reports provide information on inside directors’ shareholdings and their
annual remuneration (excluding pension and retirement benefits). This information
is hand-collected.


Measure of DAs
Total accruals ( TA ) can be decomposed into non-DAs ( NA ) and DA, with NA representing the expected (normal) accruals that would be reported without managerial
manipulation such that:


TAit = NAit + DAit (2),


where i and t are firm and period indicators, respectively.

On the basis of prior studies (Jones 1991; Dechow et al. 1995), we compute
TA as follows:


TAit = ∆ CAit - ∆ CLit - ∆ Cashit + ∆ STDit - Depit (3),


where, for sample firm i in year t,


∆ CAit = the change in current assets ( CAit - CAit - 1),

∆ CLit = the change in current liabilities ( CLit - CLit - 1),


CAR Vol. 20 No. 3 (Fall 2003)

450 Contemporary Accounting Research


∆ Cashit = the change in cash and cash equivalents ( Cashit - Cashit - 1),

∆ STDit = the change in debt included in current liabilities ( STDit - STDit - 1), and

Depit = depreciation and amortization expense.


Several approaches to measuring DAs have been used in prior studies (Dechow
et al. 1995). Guay et al. (1996) report evidence that the modified Jones 1991 model
